processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: Ingots with the nominal composition Fe-35Mn-19Al-5Cu (at.%, x = 19) were produced by melting raw materials with high purity (>99.9 %) using a vacuum induction furnace under an argon atmosphere.
The ingots were homogenized at 1200 °C for 24 h.

processing_steps.reduction_ratio: hot-rolled into plates with a thickness of 4 mm
processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: After homogenization the ingots were hot-rolled into plates with a thickness of 4 mm.
Plates were cut into 10 × 5 × 2 mm³ samples using electrical discharge machining for Vickers hardness measurements and microstructure characterizations.
The samples were solution treated at 1100 °C for 10 min under an argon atmosphere, followed by oil quenching.

The solution-treated samples were aged at temperatures between 525 °C and 650 °C for 1, 3, 6 and 10 h, followed by water quenching; this sample corresponds to aging at 600 °C for 10 h, the peak-hardness condition of the 19Al alloy.

structures.overall_structure: After aging at 600 °C for 10 h the α (BCC) matrix of the 19Al alloy had almost completely transformed into β-Mn; numerous fine BCC and FCC Cu-rich precipitates were distributed within the β-Mn / at the β-Mn interfaces.

phases_present.morphology: matrix formed by near-complete α→β-Mn transformation

precipitates.size: comparable to the FCC Cu-rich phase particles
fine particles, size comparable to the BCC phase particles
precipitates.coherency: FCC twins frequently observed within the particles

phase_interfaces.coherence: not stated (fine FCC Cu-rich particles with FCC twins at the β-Mn interfaces)

defect_interactions.qualitative_or_quantitative_description: FCC twins are frequently observed within the FCC Cu-rich particles located at the β-Mn interfaces (established by TEM/SAED on the peak-hardness alloys).

interfaces.phase_evolution: α → α + FCC Cu-rich phase → α-Mn + β-Mn + BCC phase → β-Mn + BCC phase + FCC Cu-rich phase (b0068). For the 19Al alloy, the α matrix had almost completely transformed into β-Mn after just 1 h of aging at 600 °C and above (b0053).
interfaces.interface_notes: In the peak-hardness alloys the new BCC phase and FCC Cu-rich phase formed at the interfaces between the β-Mn; the content of the FCC Cu-rich phase between β-Mn interfaces decreased gradually with increasing Al content (b0068). The β-Mn is a Mn-rich phase, so its growth enriches Mn while expelling Fe, Al and Cu to the surrounding matrix, driving formation of the BCC (Al-enriched) and Cu-rich phases at the β-Mn interfaces (b0068).

measurement_conditions.other_conditions: Vickers hardness measured with an HVS-1000 digital microhardness tester, load 9.8 N for 15 s; each sample tested 5 times and the average of 5 measurements reported.

hardness.region: bulk, 19Al aged at 600 °C for 10 h (peak-hardness condition)

measurement_conditions.specimen_geometry: mechanically polished samples (to avoid flaking of the Cu-rich phase)
measurement_conditions.other_conditions: Agilent G200 Nanoindenter, indentation depth 200 nm, each test point spaced 5 μm or more apart.

hardness.region: whole sample (average nanoindentation hardness of the hardest 19Al sample, 600 °C/10 h)
β-Mn (intrinsic hardness; indents not contacting the FCC Cu-rich and BCC phases)

measurement_conditions.specimen_geometry: Vickers indentation with radial cracks (indentation technique)
measurement_conditions.other_conditions: P = 9.8 N indentation load; average crack length c = 35 μm for the 19Al alloy; KIC calculated with Eq. (1) using E = 181 GPa and HV = 917.8.
E determined through compressive stress-strain curves.

comparative_performance.comparison_metric: peak Vickers hardness (19Al peak 917.8 HV vs 15Al peak 965.6 HV); peak hardness and fracture toughness of the ultra-hard alloys decreased with increasing Al content

characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: load 9.8 N for 15 s; each sample tested 5 times, average of 5 measurements
characterization_methods.purpose: Measure the hardness of the 19Al alloy after aging treatments
characterization_methods.key_findings: For the 19Al alloy aged at 600 °C for 10 h the Vickers hardness is 917.8 ± 24.5 HV, the peak-hardness condition of this alloy.

characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: indentation depth 200 nm; each test point spaced 5 μm or more apart; specimens mechanically polished
characterization_methods.purpose: Measure overall micro-hardness and the intrinsic hardness of β-Mn in the hardest 19Al sample
characterization_methods.key_findings: For the 19Al alloy aged at 600 °C for 10 h the average nanoindentation hardness is 10.4 ± 1.3 GPa and the intrinsic β-Mn hardness is 12.5 ± 0.4 GPa.

characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: ZEISS Sigma 300 SEM operated at 5 kV
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: β-Mn micro-area composition measured by SEM-EDS in the hardest sample
characterization_methods.purpose: Determine the chemical composition of β-Mn in the peak-hardness samples
characterization_methods.key_findings: In the hardest 19Al sample the β-Mn contains Mn 36.2 at.%, Al 17.5 at.% and Cu 2.6 at.%.

characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: Vickers indentation with radial crack-length measurement (schematic in Fig. 1)
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: P = 9.8 N; crack length measured from indentation corners; c = 0.25 Σ li; KIC from Eq. (1)
characterization_methods.purpose: Evaluate the fracture toughness (KIC) of the peak-hardness samples
characterization_methods.key_findings: For the 19Al alloy at peak hardness the average crack length is 35 μm and KIC = 3.5 MPa·m^1/2.

characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: GeminiSEM 300 SEM; scanning step size 1.5 μm (low magnification) and 0.05 μm (high magnification)
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: Electrolytically polished samples (10 % perchloric acid + 90 % ethanol)
characterization_methods.purpose: Track the evolution of constituent phases (α, β-Mn, BCC, FCC) during aging
characterization_methods.key_findings: EBSD of the 19Al alloy (e.g. 600 °C/3 h, and 650 °C/6 h) shows the phase map almost entirely β-Mn, confirming that at 600 °C and above the α matrix is nearly fully transformed to β-Mn; new BCC and FCC phases appear within the β-Mn at higher temperatures.

characterization_methods.purpose: Identify the phase compositions of the alloys after aging
characterization_methods.key_findings: XRD patterns show both α-Mn and β-Mn peaks (with α/D0₃), indicating that α-Mn and β-Mn coprecipitated during aging before the α matrix fully transformed to β-Mn; the 19Al trace reported is for the 550 °C/6 h condition.

characterization_methods.technique: Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) with SAED, HRTEM and EDS
characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: FEI Talos F200X microscope equipped with an EDS detector, operated at 200 kV
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: Ion-thinned foils; SAED/HRTEM/FFT analyses of the β-Mn and Cu-rich phases
characterization_methods.purpose: Elucidate the microstructure of the ultra-hard alloys and identify the fine interfacial precipitates
characterization_methods.key_findings: Fine FCC Cu-rich particles with FCC twins form at the β-Mn interfaces and β-Mn was poor in Cu; TEM observations reported are on the 15Al (600 °C/6 h) and 17Al (575 °C/6 h) hardest samples.

analytical_models.equation_role: KIC = 0.016 (E/HV)^(1/2) · P / c^(2/3), used to calculate the fracture toughness of the peak-hardness Fe-Mn-Al-Cu low-density steels from the indentation load and the average radial crack length c = 0.25 Σ(i=1..4) l_i.
analytical_models.model_note: Applying Eq. (1) with the above parameters for the 19Al peak-hardness sample gives KIC = 3.5 MPa·m^1/2.

unmapped_findings: The 19Al alloy needed 10 h of aging at 550 °C for the α→β-Mn transformation to complete, but at 600 °C and above the α matrix had almost completely transformed into β-Mn within just 1 h (b0053).

Peak hardness of the 19Al alloy (917.8 HV) is reached after aging at 600 °C for 10 h, which is slightly lower than the 15Al (965.6 HV) and 17Al (924.9 HV) peaks; the peak hardness after aging at higher temperatures decreased slightly with increasing Al content (b0038).
The optimal aging temperature range for achieving ultra-high hardness in the 19Al alloy is 575–625 °C (b0038).
Intrinsic hardness of β-Mn increased slightly with Al content: 12.1 ± 0.3 GPa (15Al), 12.2 ± 0.1 GPa (17Al) and 12.5 ± 0.4 GPa (19Al), attributed to solid-solution strengthening by Al (b0060).
Average crack lengths during Vickers hardness testing of the peak-hardness samples were 18 μm (15Al), 22 μm (17Al) and 35 μm (19Al) (b0061).
The ultra-hard Fe-Mn-Al-Cu low-density steels achieved a maximum specific hardness exceeding 140 HV·cm³/g while maintaining low density; the 15Al alloy reached 141 HV·cm³/g (b0073, b0077).
For the 19Al alloy aged at 650 °C for 6 h (a different condition from this sample) the volume fraction of FCC Cu-rich and BCC precipitates reached 6.5 % and the Vickers hardness was 810.9 HV (b0069).
EDS-measured composition of the 19Al alloy (Table 1): Fe 41.6, Mn 34.8, Al 18.6, Cu 5.0 (at.%) (b0013).

In aged 19Al alloys, β-Mn primarily precipitated along α grain boundaries with a small amount of short rod-shaped β-Mn within the α grains; the increase in Al content slowed the precipitation kinetics of β-Mn (b0053).
